title:
Comments of the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition in response to the Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim
Resource Adequacy Service and A Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability under ER26-3515.

documents.name: PJMICC Comments on IRAS - ER26-3515.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                :                Docket No. ER26-3515-000


                                   COMMENTS OF
                      THE PJM INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMER COALITION

        The PJM Industrial Customer Coalition (“PJMICC” or “Coalition”) respectfully submits

these Comments in response to the Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim

Resource Adequacy Service and A Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability (“IRAS

Filing”), which was filed at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

“Commission”) in the above-referenced docket.1 PJMICC is a coalition of energy-intensive

industrial and institutional customers in the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) region and is

active in PJM’s governance and stakeholder processes.

        As energy-intensive retail customers, PJMICC’s members are directly and substantially

affected by the rules governing the PJM grid and its markets, including PJM’s rules to

accommodate new large load growth. In PJMICC’s view, the rules to accommodate new large load

growth must be fair to existing customers but also crafted to support the economic growth of the

region. To that end, PJMICC offers the following Comments for Commission consideration.

                                          I.       BACKGROUND

        On August 13, 2026, PJM filed the IRAS Filing with the Commission. Also on August 13,

2026, FERC issued a Combined Notice of Filings, setting a comment deadline of September 3,

2026. PJMICC filed a doc-less Motion to Intervene on August 14, 2026.




1
  PJM Interconnection L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry
to Address System Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (Aug. 13, 2026) (“IRAS Filing”).
          PJM’s IRAS Filing proposes revisions to the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among

Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) and the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to

establish the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”). PJM’s IRAS proposal broadly

consists of five parts. First, PJM proposes to clarify a Load Serving Entity’s (“LSE”) obligation to

bring in new capacity that is equal to or greater than a New Large Load’s 2 peak load, or else be

subject to load reduction requests during emergencies.3 Second, PJM seeks to create and maintain

a Large Load Registry that will list existing Large Loads on the system and New Large Loads that

plan to interconnect in the future.4 Third, PJM proposes an IRAS product, which it describes as “a

new supplemental capacity product through which New Large Loads provide a load reduction

service” – put simply, IRAS is a curtailment tool for deployment by PJM to manage resource

adequacy shortfalls “that would otherwise drive shedding of native loads.” 5 Fourth, PJM proposes

the Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) concept as a “category of new capacity eligible

to address New Large Load capacity needs.”6 Specifically, BYONC is an incentive intended to

address new capacity needs by reducing a New Large Load’s potential IRAS requirement in

lockstep with the new capacity the New Large Load secures itself. Finally, PJM proposes to

exclude New Large Loads from the Variable Resource Requirement (“VRR”) Curve in future

Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) Auctions, to the extent they lack sufficient BYONC

provisions. PJM states that the “rest of PJM’s load should not be exposed to the price impacts




2
   New Large Load is defined, for purposes of the initial IRAS implementation, as “end-use customer load that is either
(a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1, 2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027, that
increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not
previously meet the definition of Large Load.” IRAS Filing, Attachment A. If IRAS is activated in the future, the
definition specifies different dates.
3
   IRAS Filing at 4. This load reduction request would occur prior to Pre-Emergency Load Management Response.
4
   Id. at 22.
5
   Id.
6
  Id. at 23.



                                                          2
 caused by those New Large Loads’ procurement of their capacity needs through the RPM

Auctions.”7

                       II.     INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

          PJMICC is a coalition representing industrial consumers, institutional customers, and other

large electricity users in the PJM Region. Coalition member organizations require significant

volumes of electricity and natural gas to support their operations—they include manufacturers of

paper, cement, chemicals, metals, pharmaceutical products, and consumer goods; institutional

customers such as hospitals and universities; and other large energy users. Coalition members

represent the backbone of American manufacturing and core services that support the United

States’ competitive strength in a global economy. They are anchor employers across the PJM

Region, supporting the regional economy with good-paying jobs and domestic production of goods

and services.

          For decades, PJMICC members and other similarly-situated retail customers have

contributed to system reliability and invested in resource adequacy by participation in PJM’s

capacity market, development of behind-the-meter generation, bilateral power purchase

agreements, or supporting cost-of-service regulated generation. Many Coalition members have

also made long-term investments in their on-site electrical infrastructure, strengthening the grid.

However, PJMICC is concerned that large retail customers who have contributed to resource

adequacy for many years may be required to bear costs triggered by the rapid growth of new large-

load customers. For American industry, institutions, and other traditional energy users to thrive,

their costs must be just, reasonable, and consistent with cost-causation principles.




7
    Id.



                                                   3
        To that end, the Coalition responds to the IRAS Filing with these Comments. Its

recommendations can be summarized as follows:

      First, existing large loads should be excluded from the Large Load Registry. The
       registry’s purpose is to track new large loads driving new system costs, not existing
       customers already integrated into the grid and reflected in historical forecasts. If existing
       loads are included for informational purposes, they must be clearly exempted from all
       IRAS operational obligations — including curtailment, BYONC requirements, and RPM
       auction adjustments — and any collected data must be subject to robust confidentiality
       protections.
      Second, ordinary load fluctuations should not subject existing customers to IRAS.
       PJM’s definition of “new” vs. “existing” Large Load must distinguish between genuine
       new load growth and normal operational variation at existing facilities. The baseline
       measurement should not confuse normal business operational fluctuations as being new
       load growth associated with business expansions, triggering IRAS for customers that have
       effectively been operating as existing Large Loads.
      Third, incremental expansions should trigger IRAS obligations only for the net new
       MW above 50 MW. As a threshold matter, it must be noted that very little evidence has
       been presented that 50 MW is an appropriate bright-line trigger for the obligations set forth
       by PJM’s instant filing. Many of the new computational loads are significantly in excess
       of 50 MW, whereas 50 MW is not unusual for an industrial or institutional facility. When
       an existing Large Load facility expands, only load growth over 50 MW from the baseline
       should be subject to IRAS. (That is, a 50 MW facility should not be subjected to IRAS
       until it expands beyond 100 MW.) PJM should adopt bright-line, easy-to-implement
       grandfathering rules for pre-expansion load, clear methodologies for measuring
       incremental growth, and anti-gaming provisions, while avoiding a framework that chills
       legitimate phased and planned development.
      Fourth, IRAS participants should not receive compensation that shifts costs to other
       ratepayers. Compensating new large loads for IRAS curtailment — and recovering those
       costs broadly through retail rates — directly contradicts the Ratepayer Protection Pledge’s
       commitment that new computational loads will not increase electricity costs for other
       consumers. If any compensation is provided, it should be funded by the new large-load
       customer base itself; States must retain full discretion to set the rate at zero without risking
       a violation of the filed rate doctrine.
      Finally, PJM’s “peak load” measurement in the New Large Load definition should
       align with FERC-approved retail BTMG rules. Load netted against on-site generation
       under BTMG should be measured in a similar manner for IRAS purposes, providing
       certainty to retail customers who have invested in resource adequacy through retail BTMG.

       PJMICC respectfully requests that the Commission consider these Comments in its review

of the IRAS Filing. Each of these points is set forth in greater detail below.




                                                  4
                                               III.     COMMENTS

        A.       Existing Large Loads Should Be Excluded from the Large Load Registry.

        PJM explains in the IRAS Filing that the Large Load Registry (“Registry”) will contain

information about Large Loads in the PJM Region that will “facilitate the transparent

implementation of IRAS and assist the Commission and states in monitoring whether loads are, in

fact adhering to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge (“Pledge”) commitment to ‘build, bring, or buy

the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands.’” 8

Specifically, PJM will use the Large Load Registry to identify and quantify New Large Loads by

zone or area and “allocate IRAS responsibility to each zone/area accordingly,” beginning with the

Delivery Year starting June 1, 2027.9

        PJMICC does not object to the need to track New Large Loads with IRAS responsibility.

However, PJMICC disagrees with PJM’s decision to place all Large Loads—including Existing

Large Loads—into the Registry, for the following reasons.

                      i. First, the Primary Purpose of the Registry Is To Facilitate IRAS, Which
                         Does Not Apply to Existing Large Loads.

        Existing users, including large industrial and commercial users, have historically paid for

the generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure they use. Existing large users are not

the source of the new costs driving the need for IRAS and, by extension, a Large Load Registry.

This cost causation principle, which is a foundational element of utility rate design, requires that

costs be allocated to the customers who cause them. Existing large retail customers are not driving

new infrastructure costs and should not be subjected to new tracking and potential curtailment



8
   IRAS Filing at 28 (quoting The White House, Ratepayer Protection Pledge (Mar. 4, 2026), available at
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/). PJM further notes that “‘add[ing] more
capacity that serves the broader public by increasing supply’ in order to protect ‘Americans from higher prices’” is
part of the commitment of the Pledge. Id. (quoting Ratepayer Protection Pledge).
9
  IRAS Filing at 28-29.



                                                         5
 obligations designed to address the consequences of new entrants seeking service before they can

be reliably accommodated. Therefore, existing large users should not be subject to exposure on

the proposed Large Load Registry.

                    ii. The Large Load Registry Imposes New Privacy Concerns Upon Existing
                        Large Load Customers, Without Adequate Justification.

        The Large Load Registry proposes collecting substantial operational data, raising new

privacy concerns for existing customers who should not be subject to the IRAS. Data such as

customer identity, location, in-service date, delivery point, load quantity, and backup generation

details represent confidential information that existing customers have never been required to

report in this manner. For energy-intensive industries, such as steel, air separation, paper, and

consumer goods manufacturers, knowledge of load size, location, Demand Response (“DR”)

participation, and LSE relationships enables competitors (including international competitors) to

infer critical operational intelligence. For example, publicly disclosing which DR programs a steel

mill participates in would provide competitors with insights into its operations and cost structure.

Further, in restructured states, a customer’s supplier relationship is typically confidential, and

public disclosure of retail customers’ LSEs could affect the functioning of retail markets.

        State-regulated utilities—with whom large retail customers have a direct relationship—

already have much or all of this information, but it is often subject to state confidentiality rules.

These customers’ local utilities understand the critical sensitivity of this information. It is carefully

guarded by American industry.

        While PJM may argue that including existing loads helps improve overall forecast

accuracy, the forecasting problem driving this initiative is new load growth, not existing load that

is already captured in historical data. To the extent that existing loads are included for

informational purposes, the Commission should require PJM to limit the information collected to




                                                   6
 what is necessary for loads that are not subject to IRAS. Additionally, non-IRAS load should be

clearly exempted from any operational obligations tied to the Registry, including IRAS curtailment

priorities, BYONC requirements, and RPM auction demand curve adjustments.

                  iii. Additional Substantive and Due Process Protections Are Needed If Existing
                       Large Loads Are Included in the Registry.

       PJMICC firmly argues that under no circumstances should existing Large Loads be subject

to IRAS curtailment obligations, which, by PJM’s own design, apply only to New Large Loads

that do not bring their own capacity. However, the Registry, as proposed, does not contain

provisions that ensure IRAS load is not conflated with existing load. If Existing Large Loads are

included in the Registry, the Commission should require PJM to incorporate additional

classification or disclosures within the Registry to ensure that IRAS is not assigned to loads that

are merely experiencing year-over-year normal operation fluctuations. Additionally, Registry

determinations, as currently proposed, lack clear customer notice, correction, and appeal

procedures. Per the filing, PJM may validate information with Transmission Owners and Electric

Distributors, request additional information, and “consult” with the Large Load, but the Tariff does

not establish a customer right to notice, review, correction, hearing, or appeal before classification

and eligible New Large Load amounts become operative. Unremedied errors concerning peak

load, in-service date, affiliation, site boundaries, BYONC, or Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”) allocation can directly change curtailment exposure and capacity treatment. The IRAS

Filing also invokes significant enforcement consequences for false or incomplete information

without providing a corresponding safe harbor for good faith estimates or corrections. This is

concerning for existing customers, some of whom operate complex configurations with multiple

facilities, generation integrated with industrial processes, and other nuances that may make

reporting obligations less than straightforward. Any such process should also minimize the




                                                  7
 compliance risks for retail customers that are otherwise, in many cases, not directly involved in

the PJM wholesale market.

           Further, any Registry data collected from existing customers must be subject to robust

confidentiality protection. The Registry may include site descriptions, locations, in-service

schedules, peak loads, telemetry, backup generation and permitting limits, contracts or service

agreements, and contact information. As explained above, this is highly sensitive competitive

intelligence for many retail customers. Additionally, the disclosure of this information creates

cybersecurity and commercial information risks. While the Registry is intended to administer

IRAS transparently, it must not pose operational or competitive risks due to inadequate

confidentiality safeguards. PJMICC respectfully requests that the Commission require PJM to

implement appropriate safeguards, privacy restrictions, due process, and, for non-IRAS load, limit

the amount of data required for the Registry.

           B.       Ordinary Load Fluctuations Should Not Subject Existing Retail Customers to
                    IRAS.

           As PJM states in the IRAS Filing, IRAS is designed as a “supplemental capacity product

through which New Large Loads provide a load reduction service.” 10 PJM drafted the IRAS Filing,

including the proposed definition of New Large Load, to address resource adequacy challenges on

the grid primarily driven by large load growth.

           PJMICC agrees with the focus on new and expanding load (to the extent not otherwise

considered to be “organic” load growth). However, the Coalition is concerned that, under the

proposed definition of New Large Load, existing Large Load customers may be mistakenly

deemed New Large Load solely due to ordinary load fluctuations.




10
     IRAS Filing at 22.



                                                  8
         Ordinary load fluctuations can occur for a manufacturer, for example, during a slower

production year or when weather patterns are milder than usual. To use a simple illustration,

consider a customer facility whose peak load this Delivery Year is 48 MW but whose peak load

was 54 MW in the prior two Delivery Years. If, in the next Delivery Year, this customer’s peak

load returns to 54 MW, PJM may deem it to have 6 MW of load growth. Under the New Large

Load definition, it is unclear if PJM would deem the entire facility as “New Large Load” or only

a part of it. Either way, the customer facility is merely returning to its typical historical levels after

a slow business cycle year (such as after COVID). It would not make sense to impose 6 MW (or

54 MW, if PJM fails to recognize only the incremental increase) of IRAS and Registry obligations

on a customer facility that has been paying to support resource adequacy for years, if not decades.

        This is an important issue for several reasons. First, the point of IRAS is not to burden

existing customers – even existing Large Load customers – with issues that are caused by rapid

new load growth. Second, it is important to be clear as to the rules of the road, so energy-intensive

businesses can continue to do the work it does every day without worrying about triggering

additional obligations (that are designed to accommodate the new, super-sized large load growth).

Third, incremental modernization or electrification at facilities should not create new obligations

for existing loads.

        To address this issue, PJMICC offers the following recommendation: the Commission

should require PJM to establish a “baseline” load value for existing Large Load customers based

on historic usage. Any value established for a customer should accommodate, if not facilitate,

existing Large Load customers’ ability to respond to changing grid and resource adequacy

conditions, such as, for example, moving away from “peak management” strategies toward new




                                                    9
 “Demand Response” offerings. Additionally, PJM should allow an existing retail customer to

demonstrate to PJM that load growth is actually a normal fluctuation.

        C.      Incremental Expansions Should Trigger IRAS Obligations Only for the Net
                New MW Above 50 MW.

        Another concern for existing industrial and institutional customers is what the process

looks like for incremental load growth—for example, when a university adds a new building or a

factory adds a production line.

        Currently, the proposed definition of New Large Load includes (a) “a Large Load that goes

into service after June 1, 2027” or (b) “incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027, that increases

the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site, that, prior to such incremental load,

did not previously meet the definition of Large Load.” Presumably, this would mean that a 45 MW

facility that undergoes a 10 MW expansion would be deemed New Large Load.

        This approach fundamentally puts existing large loads at a competitive disadvantage. If a

new facility can be built at 20 MW without triggering IRAS obligations, surely a 50 MW facility

that has been paying into the system for decades should be able to expand to 70 MW (an equivalent

20 MW update) on a similar basis. To obligate the latter to IRAS, but not the former, would be

unduly discriminatory against existing customers.

        Unfortunately, PJM’s proposal does not clearly address how such incremental expansions

should be treated. First, as a threshold matter, PJM must be clear that only incremental expansion

should be classified as New Large Load. The proposed definition of New Large Load includes

“incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027, that increases the existing end-use customer load

at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition

of Large Load.” While this appears to address incremental growth of existing retail customers

whose “baseline” is under 50 MW and that then expand, the definition does not expressly address




                                                  10
 situations where an existing Large Load (already >50 MW) expands. PJM should calculate a

“baseline” peak load (as discussed above) for each Large Load so that it is clear when there has

been real growth at a customer location and should then explain that only the incremental MW

becomes “New Large Load.”

        Second, the Commission should order PJM to require that, for existing Large Load

customers, only the incremental growth above and beyond 50 MW of net new load should be

classified as new load. This approach is the clearest and least discriminatory, as it avoids putting

existing retail customers who have paid for capacity at a competitive disadvantage. Without

clarification that an existing facility may add up to 50 MW of expansion without triggering IRAS

obligations, there is a distinct risk of chilling legitimate expansions. Treating the entire facility as

a New Large Load upon expansion could discourage rational, phased development at existing

facilities.

        In summary, PJM should establish clear rules for phased expansions, including the

following:

       A methodology for measuring both “baseline” peak load and incremental load growth at
        existing facilities.
       A bright-line rule that the pre-expansion load quantity is grandfathered and not subject to
        IRAS. The load would be treated as a New Large Load only after 50 MW is added to the
        customer’s baseline load.
       Provisions addressing the timing of registration obligations for expansions (i.e.,
        registration should be required only when the incremental expansion is contracted or
        committed, not when the original facility was interconnected). Additionally, PJM should
        address the potential for gaming (e.g., a customer structuring multiple sub-50 MW facilities
        within a one-mile radius to avoid the threshold) while still protecting legitimate existing
        multiple sub-50 MW operations within one-mile from being swept into the Large Load
        framework.

        These updates to PJM’s proposal would provide significant protections for existing retail

customers and avoid stifling economic investment by American manufacturing, education and

medical institutions, and other existing large retail customers.


                                                  11
         D.       IRAS Participants Should Not Receive Compensation That Shifts Costs to
                 Other Ratepayers

        PJM proposes that New Large Loads subject to IRAS curtailment during grid emergencies

would receive wholesale compensation at a maximum rate equal to 50% of the Non-Performance

Charge Rate.11 PJM also proposes that Large Loads may waive such compensation consistent with

any Large Loads’ signing of the Pledge.12

        PJM does not propose a specific cost recovery mechanism for IRAS compensation, stating

that cost recovery “will be left to the Electric Distributors that directed the specific load reductions

to implement IRAS, consistent with their state-approved program.” 13 PJM states that “[w]hether a

specific New Large Load may be entitled to compensation for provision of IRAS will be

determined by state authorities under state law….”14

        Unfortunately, PJM’s approach is flawed. By establishing a FERC-jurisdictional payment

obligation to IRAS load, PJM creates tensions with the Pledge and the filed rate doctrine and will

make it particularly difficult for States to protect existing customers from having to pay IRAS

customers for their reductions.

                      i. PJM’s Proposed Compensation Is Inconsistent with the Ratepayer
                         Protection Pledge.

        The Ratepayer Protection Pledge (“Pledge”) Proclamation, issued by the President on

March 4, 2026, provides that “data centers’ energy needs will not increase household electricity

costs for American citizens” and that data center companies “will build, bring, or buy the new

generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their energy demands, and pay for all new

power delivery infrastructure upgrades.”15 The Pledge itself states that “Companies will build,


11
   IRAS Filing at 102.
12
   Id. at 17, 102.
13
   Id. at 106.
14
   Id.
15
   Proclamation No. 11014, 91 Fed. Reg. 11439 (Mar. 4, 2026).



                                                      12
 bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy

demands, paying the full cost of those resources whether by building, or buying from, new or

otherwise additive power plants.”16

        At heart, the Pledge’s commitment is to consumer protection. The Pledge contemplates

that data centers bear their own costs, not receive payments from the system after failing to bring

their own capacity. The Pledge’s framework is premised on data centers paying their own way. If

new data center loads that do not bring their own capacity receive IRAS compensation recovered

through retail rates, that cost is shifted to other ratepayers—directly contradicting the Pledge’s

commitment that data centers will not increase electricity costs for other consumers. In fact, the

risk that these costs are shifted to large retail, industrial, and institutional customers is heightened,

because many States are focused primarily on preventing cost shifts to residential customers.

However, curtailment of IRAS load should not be compensated by other ratepayers (whether

residential, small commercial, or industrial/institutional); rather, it is the condition upon which a

New Large Load can begin taking service sooner without bringing matching capacity to the

system.

                     ii. PJM’s Approach to IRAS Compensation Creates Filed Rate Doctrine and
                         Consumer Protection Risks for States.

        Once FERC approves a wholesale rate—such as the maximum IRAS compensation rate—

it is difficult for States to set rates inconsistent with FERC-jurisdictional rates. As a legal matter,

States may not undermine FERC-jurisdictional rates. 17 However, States are also limited, as a

practical matter of rate setting, in allocating rates in a manner inconsistent with the underlying




16
   The White House, Ratepayer Protection Pledge (Mar. 4, 2026), available at
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.
17
   See, e.g., Nantahala Power & Light Co. v. Thornburg, 476 U.S. 953 (1986); Mississippi Power & Light Co. v.
Mississippi ex rel. Moore, 487 U.S. 354 (1988).



                                                       13
 wholesale costs. Consequently, if FERC approves a maximum wholesale compensation rate for

IRAS, states may be constrained in their ability to decline to pass through those costs or to set

retail rates that nullify the compensation. Although PJM characterizes IRAS compensation as

subject to state discretion, a FERC-approved wholesale rate may create a federal floor that states

cannot easily undercut. Additionally, this creates tension with state consumer protection efforts. A

FERC-approved IRAS compensation rate could interfere with these state-level consumer

protection measures. Acknowledging the exigent circumstances that exist, PJMICC offers that a

reasonable alternative may be for PJM’s Tariff to remain silent on IRAS compensation and allow

states to consider programmatic approaches to compensation for any IRAS curtailments.

           E.      PJM’s Definition of New Large Load Should Track with PJM’s BTMG Rules.

           In the IRAS Filing, PJM mentions co-located load, but it does not explain how Behind-

the-Meter Generation (“BTMG”) rules interact with IRAS obligations. 18 In PJM’s Co-Located

Load proceeding before the FERC, the Commission has ordered PJM to maintain Behind-the-

Meter Generation (“BTMG”) rules for retail BTMG up to 50 MW. 19 The Commission should

require PJM to clarify that its measurement of “peak load” in the proposed definition of New

Large Load should track with retail BTMG rules approved by the Commission. For example, if

an 80 MW load with 50 MW of generation is tagged at 30 MW pursuant to retail BTMG rules, it

should be considered 30 MW for purposes of IRAS, as well. This approach will provide certainty

and consistency to retail customers who have invested in resource adequacy through retail

BTMG.




18
     See IRAS Filing at 36.
19
     195 FERC ¶ 61,209 (Order entered Jun. 18, 2026) at PP 207-220.



                                                        14
                                       IV.     CONCLUSION

       PJMICC respectfully urges the Commission to require PJM to implement the safeguards

and clarifications described above in its IRAS proposal. These measures would go a long way to

ensuring the IRAS program is just and reasonable and that existing retail customers are protected,

consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

                                             Respectfully submitted,
